scenario: Community search over short user-generated posts, questions, answers and comments. Key metrics are search relevance (nDCG) and CTR. Focus: semantic matching, query understanding, short-text retrieval, ranking models and LLM applications in search.

papers.title: ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling
papers.authors: Wenhao Li, Qinglin Jia, Chenghou Jin, Zihong Xian, Jiezhou Ji, Yanzhi Liu, Zezheng Wang, Ruiming Tang, Chaoyi Ma, Zhaojie Liu, Wenwu Ou
papers.summary: ECHO makes 100K-event histories affordable by retaining reusable original records before candidate-aware retrieval. A full-history teacher supervises selection, while retrieval and aggregation share relevance parameters. Kuaishou reports a 0.613% increase in app usage time in an online test.
papers.key_insight: Compression can preserve individually addressable events rather than only latent interest vectors. Reusable user-level selection moves work out of the request path and leaves candidate-specific matching to a smaller evidence set.

deep_reading.title: ECHO: Efficient Cascade with Homogeneous Operators for Distillation-Guided 100K-Sequence Modeling
deep_reading.content:
ECHO (Kuaishou) is a three-stage funnel: 100K raw behaviors → a user-side learned top-K (candidate-agnostic, computed outside the request path and cached per user) keeps 10K → each candidate runs GSU-style retrieval for 100 → target attention aggregates them for the ranker. Because the user-side selector never sees the candidate, it is trained by knowledge distillation from a target-attention teacher that sees the full history and the candidate, plus a boundary loss that pushes "teacher-preferred but not in top-K" events over the cut. Retrieval and the final attention reuse the teacher's relevance parameters; that is the "Homogeneous Operators" in the title. By the paper's analytical estimate, sequence-branch FLOPs are ~160× lower than STCA; GAUC on KuaiRand Comment improves 1.520% relative to the strongest baseline, and a 7-day online A/B test shows +0.613% app usage time.

## 1. Architecture: what each funnel stage does

This section shows how 100K events shrink to a size the ranker can afford.

Four terms used throughout:

- **Target attention**: attention with the candidate as query and history events as keys/values. It outputs a candidate-specific interest vector. DIN is the classic example.
- **GSU / ESU**: SIM's two-stage design. The General Search Unit retrieves a few relevant events with a light scorer. The Exact Search Unit runs full target attention over them.
- **Top-K**: keep the K highest-scoring positions.
- **Knowledge distillation (KD)**: train a student to match a teacher's output distribution.

| Stage | Module | In → out | Sees candidate? | Runs where | Training signal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ① User-side compression | Distilled Selector (DS) | 100K → 10K raw records | No | Real-time training, written to a store | KD + boundary loss |
| ② Candidate retrieval | TFR, TWIN-style GSU | 10K → 100 per candidate | Yes | Online request | Ranking loss; scorer params from teacher |
| ③ Aggregation | TWIN-style ESU | 100 → interest vector | Yes | Online request | Multi-task ranking loss |
| Teacher | Full-history target attention | Full history + training targets | Yes | Training only | Its own prediction loss |

TFR stands for Target-aware Fine-grained Retriever, the stage-two retriever.

Two graphs train concurrently. The selector graph trains the teacher and DS; DS writes each user's top-K records to an intermediate store. The ranking graph reads those records and trains TFR, aggregation and the ranker.

Online requests only read the store. They never run DS or touch the 100K history.

DS keeps original records: item ID, timestamp, side features. C-Former and SequenceO1 compress history into latent tokens; each ECHO record stays individually matchable.

![ECHO framework: the selector graph writes top-K records during real-time training; the ranking graph reads them online.](figs/2610.28569/architecture.svg)

## 2. Walk-through: one request through three stages (illustrative numbers)

This section ties the table together with one example. All numbers here are illustrative, not from the paper.

User A has 80,000 events. During real-time training overnight, DS scores all 80,000 and stores the top 10,000. One of them is a fishing video A finished eight months ago.

At 9 a.m. A opens the feed. The ranker must score 500 candidates, one of which is a new fishing-gear video.

Stage one is already done. The ranker reads A's 10,000 records once; all 500 candidates share them.

Stage two: TFR uses the fishing-gear video as query, scores the 10,000 records and keeps the top 100. The eight-month-old fishing video scores high and is retrieved.

Stage three: target attention weights those 100 records. Fishing-related events get large weights, the interest vector goes into the ranking tower, which predicts click, like, comment and so on.

Had DS dropped that fishing record, stage two could never find it. That is why DS needs teacher supervision.

## 3. Title keywords mapped to modules

**Cascade**: the 100K → 10K → 100 → attention budgets. 10K bounds interest coverage; 100 bounds per-candidate compute.

**Homogeneous Operators**: TWIN shares relevance parameters between GSU and ESU. ECHO goes one step further: the teacher's learned query/key relevance parameters $\Theta_{rel}$ are exported to both TFR and the final target attention. All three use one scoring operator, so coarse retrieval and fine aggregation agree on what "relevant" means.

**Distillation-Guided**: DS is trained from the teacher (Section 4).

**100K-Sequence Modeling**: online raw history is capped at 100K events.

## 4. Training DS: scoring, distillation, boundary loss

This section solves stage one's core problem: DS cannot see the candidate but must pre-select events useful for candidates.

### 4.1 DS scoring

$$s^S_j = \frac{1}{H_s}\sum_{h=1}^{H_s}\langle W^S_{Q,h}\, e,\; W^S_{K,h}\, z^S_j\rangle$$

Symbols: $s^S_j$ is the student's (DS) score for event $j$; $e$ is a user vector built only from profile features; $z^S_j$ encodes event $j$ (features plus timestamp); $W^S_{Q,h}$, $W^S_{K,h}$ are head-$h$ query/key projections; $H_s$ is the number of heads.

Intuition: attention scoring with the user as query. No candidate is involved, so one set of scores serves every candidate and can be cached. DS keeps the top $K$ positions, $\mathcal{I}^K$; in production $K = 10{,}000$.

### 4.2 Teacher scoring

$$s^T_{v,j} = \frac{1}{H_t}\sum_{h=1}^{H_t}\langle W^T_{Q,h}\, f_T(c, x_v),\; W^T_{K,h}\, z^T_j\rangle$$

Symbols: $s^T_{v,j}$ is the teacher's score for event $j$ given candidate $v$; $f_T(c, x_v)$ encodes context $c$ and candidate features $x_v$ into a query; $z^T_j$ is the teacher's own event encoding (not shared with DS).

Intuition: a standard full-history target attention. It knows the candidate, so its scores say which history truly matters for that candidate.

### 4.3 Distillation loss

$$\mathcal{L}_{KD} = -\frac{T^2}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{j=1}^{L_b}\mathrm{sg}\big[p^T_{b,j}\big]\log p^S_{b,j}$$

Symbols: $\mathcal{B}$ is a batch and $b$ one user–candidate sample; $L_b$ is that user's history length; $p^T_{b,j}$, $p^S_{b,j}$ are teacher and student softmax probabilities over history positions at temperature $T$; $\mathrm{sg}$ is stop-gradient, so the student loss never updates the teacher.

Intuition: soft-label cross-entropy. A user has several training candidates, each with its own teacher distribution, but the student has one score vector, so it fits what those distributions share. It learns to rank events useful for most candidates first.

### 4.4 Boundary loss

Even after distribution matching, a few teacher-preferred events can sit outside the student's top-K. The boundary loss targets them.

Three steps. Compute a sharper teacher distribution $\tilde p^T$ with temperature $T_m < T$. Outside the top-K, take the $n$ positions with the highest teacher probability, $j^+$ (missed positives); inside it, take the $n$ lowest, $j^-$ (placeholder negatives). Pair them by rank:

$$\omega_{b,i} = \mathrm{sg}\Big[\max\big(\tilde p^T_{b,j^+_{b,i}} - \tilde p^T_{b,j^-_{b,i}},\; 0\big)\Big]$$

$$\mathcal{L}_{aux} = \frac{\sum_{b}\sum_{i} \omega_{b,i}\; \mathrm{softplus}\big((s^S_{b,j^-_{b,i}} - s^S_{b,j^+_{b,i}} + \delta)/T_{rank}\big)}{\sum_{b}\sum_{i} \omega_{b,i} + \epsilon}$$

Symbols: $i$ indexes pairs; $\omega_{b,i}$ is the pair weight, the teacher's preference gap (clipped at 0); $s^S$ is the student score; $\delta$ is the desired margin; $T_{rank}$ scales the loss; $\epsilon$ avoids division by zero.

Intuition: a weighted pairwise ranking loss acting only at the top-K boundary. It pushes "should be in" events up and "taking a slot without mattering" events down, harder when the teacher's preference gap is larger. Pairs and weights are detached, so no gradient flows through the discrete top-K.

### 4.5 Full objective

$$\mathcal{L}_{sel} = \alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{pred} + \beta\,\mathcal{L}_{KD} + \gamma\,\mathcal{L}_{aux}$$

Symbols: $\mathcal{L}_{pred}$ is the teacher's multi-task prediction loss; $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ are weights.

Intuition: $\mathcal{L}_{pred}$ updates only the teacher, keeping it current on what is relevant; $\mathcal{L}_{KD}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{aux}$ update only DS. Both train live in the same stream; the teacher is not frozen. The ranking graph uses its own $\mathcal{L}_{rank}$.

## 5. Deployment: three engineering optimizations

**Common-feature sharing.** Samples of one user in a batch load the long history into GPU memory once.

**Compact record encoding.** Eight int64 fields cost 64 bytes per record, 640 KB at 10K records. ECHO packs each field into a fixed width sized to its value range.

**Move the key projection to the query side.** Standard target attention projects every history event into a key, so online cost or key-cache size grows with history length. ECHO uses:

$$\langle q W_Q,\; h W_K\rangle = \langle (q W_Q) W_K^{\top},\; h\rangle$$

Symbols: $q$ is the candidate-side query vector; $h$ is one history event vector; $W_Q$, $W_K$ are the projection matrices.

Intuition: multiply $W_K$ into the query once per request; history vectors enter the dot product directly, with no per-event projection and no key cache.

## 6. Experiments

**Baselines.** DIN: target attention over the latest 100 events. SIM: GSU/ESU retrieval. TWIN: SIM with shared GSU/ESU parameters. STCA: end-to-end stacked target-aware cross-attention (trained at ~2K, extrapolated to 10K). TWIN V2: clusters the latest 50K events into ~10K units. SequenceO1: a fixed 100-token sketch. GAUC is per-user AUC, weighted-averaged.

| Result | Numbers | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| KuaiRand-1K Comment GAUC | 0.6252 → 0.6347 (+1.520%, best baseline SequenceO1) | Largest public-data gain; best on all 8 tasks |
| Industrial Comment GAUC | 0.7824 → 0.7851 (+0.345%, best baseline TWIN V2) | Industrial gains 0.113%–0.345% |
| By history length (vs TWIN) | <10K users +0.045%, >50K users +1.279% | Learned selection matters more as history grows |
| Teacher top-100 recall | DS 99.976%, recency 57.905%, random 49.443% | DS almost never drops what the teacher values most |
| Older events selected | 46.08% outside the latest 10K | DS picks relevant, not recent |
| Sequence-branch FLOPs (L=100K) | 160.3× (train), 159.2× (infer) below STCA | Analytical, sequence branch only; no end-to-end latency |
| Long-history accuracy (50K) | STCA 0.6645, ECHO 0.6630 | Full modeling is slightly better; ECHO gets most of it at ~1/160 compute |
| Ablation: no KD, no boundary loss | Comment 0.6200 → 0.6347 (+2.371%) | Teacher supervision is what makes DS work |
| Online A/B (7 days, 5% traffic) | Usage time +0.613%, per user +0.640% | Incremental over a system with TWIN and SequenceO1-like compression |

1.520% is relative: $(0.6347 - 0.6252) / 0.6252 \approx 1.52\%$; the absolute gap is 0.0095. The ablation removes both losses together, so the boundary loss alone is not isolated.

![Left: teacher top-100 recall within the 10K retained set; right: retained teacher relevance mass.](figs/2610.28569/echo_history_preservation_merged_20261020.svg)

![Top: analytical sequence-branch FLOPs vs. history length; bottom: GAUC from a separate length study.](figs/2610.28569/echo_stca_scaling_rq_original_style_corrected.svg)

## 7. Limitations

The 100K → 10K cut is hard. Events DS drops cannot be recovered by TFR; the authors note extremely long-tail candidates may suffer.

DS updates with real-time training and store refresh, so new interests enter after a delay.

Retention quality for new users, interest shifts and new candidate types is not evaluated separately. The industrial data is not public.

## 8. Practical takeaways

**Add a user-side top-K before the GSU** and compare it with recency and random at the same storage budget.

**Monitor retention quality** offline with teacher top-100 recall and attention-mass coverage.

**Reuse an existing model as teacher** and export its query/key parameters to both GSU and ESU.

**Use the key-projection identity on its own** in any online target attention.

**Define refresh metrics**: delay for new events to enter top-K, model/store version compatibility, rollback.

Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.28569v1 . Numbers and formulas are from the paper; walk-through numbers are illustrative; practical advice is our analysis.

papers.title: KuaFu: Compressing Long User Behavior into Understanding at Billion Scale
papers.authors: Jiahao Hui, Lin Zhu, Ben Tan, Yishen Hu, Jingdong Shu, Zetai Jiang, Xining Ran, Yeshou Cai, Gong Chen, Haijie Gu
papers.summary: KuaFu avoids repeatedly encoding the same content across users and profiling tasks. It caches compact item representations, assembles them chronologically and uses staged training to preserve evidence. Tencent reports a 1.37% overall GMV increase against a long-term holdout.
papers.key_insight: Make items the unit of reuse. Encode shared content once, while preserving actions and sequence order on the user side. The cache then scales with item inventory, supporting more frequent multi-task profile refreshes.

deep_reading.title: KuaFu: Compressing Long User Behavior into Understanding at Billion Scale
deep_reading.content:
KuaFu compresses an item once and reuses that representation wherever the item appears in user histories. Interest extraction and profiling tasks then read chronologically assembled compressed sequences. Tencent uses this separation to make long-history understanding cheaper and refresh profiles more frequently at billion-user scale.

## 1. Motivation: repeated encoding across users and tasks

Separate profiling tasks often reread the same behavior history. Content interests, shopping interests and occupation inference may each invoke a model over overlapping item text. That duplicates work both across tasks and across users who consumed the same content.

Compressing an entire user history has its own costs. New interactions may require rebuilding the summary, while aggressive compression can lose rare interests or temporal relationships. The paper distinguishes fabrication, omission, date misattribution and broken reasoning, showing why final recommendation quality alone is insufficient to evaluate compression.

KuaFu shares item-side computation while retaining action and chronological structure when constructing the user input. It is an asynchronous understanding and profile-refresh system, rather than a requirement to call an LLM for every online ranking request.

## 2. Method: item compression, compact caching and chronological decoding

![Item representations are computed once; user-side assembly restores the behavior sequence for downstream understanding.](figs/2609.31045/fig1_overview.png)

A compressor reads an item's text and appends learned memory tokens. Their hidden states carry the compressed information. These are continuous vectors, rather than discrete product identifiers.

A two-axis projector reduces both the number of vectors and their width. The paper's example reduces eight memory vectors to two and the width from 2,560 to 128. The cache stores only the compact core; a lightweight up-projection restores the width expected by the decoder.

A pooled residual stabilizes early training and decays away. This matters operationally: inference must not require the original wide states if the compact cache is to deliver its storage benefit.

The decoder consumes chronological item representations alongside ordinary instructions and action information. Sharing item representations does not imply identical user profiles. The consumed items, action types and sequence order still distinguish users.

![The compressor creates memory, the projector shrinks the cached core, and the decoder reads reconstructed user sequences.](figs/2609.31045/fig2_arch.svg)

Training proceeds through reconstruction, preference-understanding post-training, joint compression-generation training and hallucination-aware reinforcement learning. Reconstruction teaches the memory to preserve information with the decoder frozen. Question answering then focuses compression on evidence useful for understanding. Joint training adapts both ends of the interface.

The final stage freezes the compressor and projector while updating the decoder. Rewards penalize specific errors and reward completeness, discouraging a trivial strategy of saying less. Judgments compare outputs against original text, rather than relying only on the compressed input.

A curriculum gradually increases history difficulty. Ablations show optimization problems when all lengths are mixed immediately, and poorer generalization without inheriting earlier training stages. Compression and the ability to read its output need coordinated training.

## 3. Contribution: representation dependencies determine cache reuse

Reuse works because an item's cached representation does not depend on a particular user or downstream task. Updating a user's behavior mainly changes the assembled input, whereas changed item content requires an item-cache update. The representation bank therefore scales with inventory rather than a separate long-history state for every user-task combination.

KuaFu also evaluates representation fidelity directly. It asks whether compressed inputs preserve retrievable events, dates and grounded conclusions. Such intermediate checks can expose damage earlier than an expensive end-to-end production experiment.

Compression ratios require careful denominators. The projector example changes 8×2,560 elements into 2×128, an 80-fold reduction. Shortening the decoder's input relative to raw text is a different quantity. Neither is automatically the whole-service cost reduction.

## 4. Results: efficiency funds longer histories and faster refreshes

The table selects four production outcomes. Interest tasks use F1, while stable profile attributes use classification accuracy. They should not be interpreted as a single common metric.

| Task | Metric | Previous online model | KuaFu |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Content interest | F1 | 85.9 | 86.5 |
| E-commerce interest | F1 | 95.7 | 96.1 |
| Occupation | Accuracy | 86.7 | 87.6 |
| Life stage | Accuracy | 76.0 | 78.0 |

Content-interest throughput rises from 40 to 180 requests per minute per GPU. That is a 350% increase, calculated as (180−40)/40, or 4.5 times the original throughput. The paper reports 190 decoder-side GPUs saved across independently provisioned tasks; the single-task multiplier should not be applied to all hardware.

On public recommendation evaluation, the compressed 4B model improves over its same-size backbone, supporting a representation effect beyond model scale. The CDs subset is an exception where compression underperforms. Public reading-comprehension and private profiling benchmarks also follow different protocols, so their gains should remain separate.

![Inspect both fabrication and completeness: fewer errors should not merely reflect omitted answers.](figs/2609.31045/fig5_rl.svg)

After hallucination-aware training, fabrication falls from 33.5% to 4.5% while overall completeness remains nearly unchanged. Independent model judging and human-agreement checks strengthen the evaluation, though they do not establish coverage of every production failure.

The online experiment randomizes by unique visitor and keeps the end-to-end resource budget equal. Treatment uses compression savings to cover a longer history and refresh profiles more often. Overall GMV increases by 1.37%, with a positive confidence interval. Because the control has a shorter history and slower refresh cadence, this supports the complete profile upgrade rather than isolating a projector or training-stage effect.

## 5. Limitations: shared representations encode shared trade-offs

The authors identify fixed task-family compression ratios as a limitation. Information-dense content may need more memory than short items, making adaptive compression a natural next step.

Industrial logs and training data cannot be released. External reproduction is limited to public benchmarks and disclosed implementation details. Some private evaluations also rely on model judges and inherit their biases.

Cache versioning is an additional engineering concern. Item edits, compressor upgrades or decoder-interface changes require a compatibility policy. Shared encoding reduces duplicate work, but an incorrect item representation can affect many users. This is an architectural implication, not a production incident reported by the paper.

## 6. Practical implications

Measure how often the same text is encoded across user histories and tasks. The economics of item-side caching depend on actual reuse, edit frequency and storage cost, not just a large user count.

Evaluate interest labels, temporal attribution and event recovery separately. A representation sufficient for occupation inference may be inadequate for explaining a recent click. Task-specific fidelity checks identify where shared compression is appropriate.

Keep representation, history coverage and refresh cadence distinguishable in experiments. Holding two fixed while changing the third helps explain how saved compute reaches business outcomes. KuaFu demonstrates one useful path from efficiency to better update capability.

Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.31045v2 . First submitted September 25, 2026; this run discovered the October revision. Calculations and deployment suggestions are editorial analysis.
deep_reading.content_html:
KuaFu compresses an item once and reuses that representation wherever the item appears in user histories. Interest extraction and profiling tasks then read chronologically assembled compressed sequences. Tencent uses this separation to make long-history understanding cheaper and refresh profiles more frequently at billion-user scale.

1. Motivation: repeated encoding across users and tasks

Separate profiling tasks often reread the same behavior history. Content interests, shopping interests and occupation inference may each invoke a model over overlapping item text. That duplicates work both across tasks and across users who consumed the same content.

Compressing an entire user history has its own costs. New interactions may require rebuilding the summary, while aggressive compression can lose rare interests or temporal relationships. The paper distinguishes fabrication, omission, date misattribution and broken reasoning, showing why final recommendation quality alone is insufficient to evaluate compression.

KuaFu shares item-side computation while retaining action and chronological structure when constructing the user input. It is an asynchronous understanding and profile-refresh system, rather than a requirement to call an LLM for every online ranking request.

2. Method: item compression, compact caching and chronological decoding

A compressor reads an item's text and appends learned memory tokens. Their hidden states carry the compressed information. These are continuous vectors, rather than discrete product identifiers.

A two-axis projector reduces both the number of vectors and their width. The paper's example reduces eight memory vectors to two and the width from 2,560 to 128. The cache stores only the compact core; a lightweight up-projection restores the width expected by the decoder.

A pooled residual stabilizes early training and decays away. This matters operationally: inference must not require the original wide states if the compact cache is to deliver its storage benefit.

The decoder consumes chronological item representations alongside ordinary instructions and action information. Sharing item representations does not imply identical user profiles. The consumed items, action types and sequence order still distinguish users.

Training proceeds through reconstruction, preference-understanding post-training, joint compression-generation training and hallucination-aware reinforcement learning. Reconstruction teaches the memory to preserve information with the decoder frozen. Question answering then focuses compression on evidence useful for understanding. Joint training adapts both ends of the interface.

The final stage freezes the compressor and projector while updating the decoder. Rewards penalize specific errors and reward completeness, discouraging a trivial strategy of saying less. Judgments compare outputs against original text, rather than relying only on the compressed input.

A curriculum gradually increases history difficulty. Ablations show optimization problems when all lengths are mixed immediately, and poorer generalization without inheriting earlier training stages. Compression and the ability to read its output need coordinated training.

3. Contribution: representation dependencies determine cache reuse

Reuse works because an item's cached representation does not depend on a particular user or downstream task. Updating a user's behavior mainly changes the assembled input, whereas changed item content requires an item-cache update. The representation bank therefore scales with inventory rather than a separate long-history state for every user-task combination.

KuaFu also evaluates representation fidelity directly. It asks whether compressed inputs preserve retrievable events, dates and grounded conclusions. Such intermediate checks can expose damage earlier than an expensive end-to-end production experiment.

Compression ratios require careful denominators. The projector example changes 8×2,560 elements into 2×128, an 80-fold reduction. Shortening the decoder's input relative to raw text is a different quantity. Neither is automatically the whole-service cost reduction.

papers.title: EASformer: Environment-Action-State Alignment for Industrial Generative Ranking
papers.authors: Bohao Li, Dinglun Cao, Pengcheng Huang, Yingda Tang, Zhiting Zhao, Yi Cao, Jilei Fu, Miao Yan, Tianying Liu, Heng Chang, Bowen Du
papers.summary: EASformer addresses a mismatch between historical tokens containing observed actions and candidates with no observed action. It separates environment, action and state before matching them. The larger of two reported online eCPM lifts is 3.94%.
papers.key_insight: Attention should compare semantically aligned representations. Separating environmental matching from action prediction also lets masked historical actions reuse the candidate-prediction pathway for self-supervision.

papers.title: SPAR: Stepwise Personalized Autoregressive Recommendation with Prefix-Balanced Semantic IDs
papers.authors: Chunrui Zhang, Gaoyun Lin, Chang Zhou, Zheng Hu, Qiran Song, Shimin Cai, Tao Zhou
papers.summary: SPAR reduces early branch errors in semantic-ID recommendation by retrieving user evidence at every decoding step and balancing traffic across sibling branches. A Youku online experiment reports a 3.95% increase in average watch time per user.
papers.key_insight: Personalization should change with the generated prefix. Inspect user-evidence retrieval and branch-load imbalance together to diagnose early decoding errors that prevent the right item from remaining reachable.

papers.title: Robustness Analysis of Pareto-based Joint Evaluation of Fairness and Relevance in Recommender Systems
papers.authors: Theresia Veronika Rampisela, Maria Maistro, Tuukka Ruotsalo, Christina Lioma
papers.summary: This study jointly evaluates recommendation relevance and fairness using distance to a data-derived Pareto frontier. Experiments on six real-world datasets test robustness and show that existing joint metrics can disagree with the frontier-based evaluation.
papers.key_insight: A multi-objective score needs an explicit reference boundary. Distance to an achievable trade-off makes the evaluation easier to interpret, while the choice of which frontier region matters remains a business decision.

papers.title: Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling?
papers.authors: Aleksandr V. Petrov, Praveen Chandar, Paul N. Bennett, Hugues Bouchard, Mounia Lalmas
papers.summary: Spotify compares pairwise transition models and Transformer recommenders under shared splits and evaluation protocols. On four of five benchmarks, at least one pairwise model outperforms both Transformer reproductions.
papers.key_insight: Useful history does not prove that higher-order interactions are necessary. Smoothed transitions and recency weighting deserve strong baseline status when attributing gains to a new sequence architecture.

papers.title: MOSS: A Production Framework for Monitoring and Diagnosing Semantic Failures in Search and Recommendation Systems
papers.authors: Alina Nesen, Prathyusha Kanmanth Reddy, David Relyea, Rohit Avinash Mujumdar, Samaneh Karimi, Bo Shen, Jordan Hashemi
papers.summary: MOSS continuously samples, scores and diagnoses semantic failures in production discovery systems. Strategy-aware prompts connect relevance judgments to actionable alerts. An offline evaluation of a backfill-blending fix reports a 76.4% reduction in alert rate.
papers.key_insight: Monitoring must understand the intended recommendation relationship. A recurring loop of targeted sampling, strategy-specific prompts and diagnostic follow-up can expose serving defects. The reported alert reduction is an offline repair estimate, not an online CTR lift.

venue.name: RecSys
venue.label: RecSys 2026 Workshop
venue.evidence: A prior version of this work was presented at the non-archival Unified Search and Recommendation Workshop (USRW), co-located with ACM RecSys 2026

papers.title: Neighborhood-Aware Unlearning for Generative Recommendation
papers.authors: Pierre Lubitzsch, Yubao Tang, Maarten de Rijke, Sebastian Schelter
papers.summary: Unlearning interactions in a semantic-ID recommender can damage neighboring items that share tokens. Neighborhood-Aware Unlearning controls local probability redistribution while removing the target behavior. Across evaluated settings, it retains more than 95% of retrained-reference utility.
papers.key_insight: Global recommendation metrics can hide local damage. Audit both forgotten interactions and their shared-code neighborhoods when removing spam or withdrawn behavior, and constrain the redistribution rather than repairing only global utility.

papers.title: Multimodal Reranking Is a System One Decision
papers.authors: Zhuchenyang Liu, Yao Zhang, Yu Xiao
papers.summary: This work ranks multimodal candidates by reading option probabilities from a single choice question instead of asking separate yes/no questions. On image retrieval, the choice format gains 5.4–7.3 Hit@1 points over per-candidate yes/no scoring.
papers.key_insight: Joint comparison provides a useful relative signal. For multimodal UGC reranking, one candidate-set decision can avoid inconsistent independent scores, but its value depends on the candidate set, image budget and latency.

papers.title: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
papers.summary: OpenAI describes a stateful ad session that follows intent across conversational turns. A separate delivery service invokes retrieval, ranking, relevance and auction tools. The article explains three central architecture choices but gives no controlled CTR comparison.
papers.key_insight: Maintaining evolving user state changes the quality of ranking inputs. Separating ad selection from answer generation supports independent delivery constraints and reduces redundant work; the evidence here is architectural rather than an attributed ranking lift.
